narrative:
# Weekly Multi-Asset Technology & Growth Strategy Briefing

The past week delivered an unusually sharp set of cross-currents across technology, growth, and cyclicals, with pronounced factor reversals inside semiconductors, software, and defensives. While the broader risk backdrop was relatively constructive, leadership within our 184-name watchlist concentrated in a handful of high-beta subsectors, particularly legacy semiconductors and select enterprise software, even as prior defensives and some medical device names lagged hard. The tape appears to be leaning back toward a reflationary, growth‑and‑productivity narrative, with investors rewarding operating leverage, cyclical AI beneficiaries, and idiosyncratic re-rating stories, while punishing crowded defensives and certain gold and materials exposures. Against this backdrop, we remain constructive but increasingly selective, leaning into names and subsectors where the week’s move is either the early innings of a multi-quarter rerating or a dislocation that improves risk‑reward.

## Market Overview

This week’s price action across the watchlist was characterized by a pronounced rotation into cyclically sensitive technology and high-operating-leverage software, with semiconductors and data storage standing out as key winners and defensive areas such as consumer staples and gold-related miners under pressure. Within semis and adjacent hardware, Intel (INTC) rallied 20.7% on the week and an extraordinary 107.4% over the past month, signaling a material change in market perception toward its foundry and AI positioning. Seagate (STX) advanced 24.0% over the week and 71.8% over the month, while Micron (MU) added 9.2% for the week and 47.4% for the month, underscoring investor conviction that AI-driven memory and storage demand is both durable and underappreciated. In parallel, Arm (ARM) fell 10.1% on the week despite a 36.2% gain over the past month, and Teradyne (TER) declined 17.4% on the week even while still up 10.6% over the month, highlighting continued factor volatility and profit-taking in some of the earlier AI winners.

Software and application platforms also delivered robust performance, especially within communication and collaboration tools and workflow platforms, suggesting renewed investor focus on durable subscription models, AI-enabled productivity gains, and improving fiscal-year guidance. Twilio (TWLO) surged 27.5% this week, now up 40.5% on the month, while Atlassian (TEAM) climbed 24.2% for the week and 28.1% for the month, and Zoom (ZM) advanced 12.4% and 28.2% over the same horizons. These moves were complemented by solid gains in Monday.com (MNDY), up 7.3% on the week and 6.8% on the month, and Workday (WDAY), up 6.0% on the week, collectively signaling a market that is re-rating high‑quality, recurring-revenue platforms after a period of valuation compression.

On the mega-cap tech front, Alphabet (GOOG) delivered an 11.9% weekly gain and a 29.9% gain over the month, reinforcing the narrative that its AI execution and cloud monetization trajectory are being reassessed positively by investors. Meta Platforms (META) moved the other way on a short-term basis, down 9.8% on the week but still up 5.1% on the month, an example of near‑term profit-taking in a name that has been a structural AI and digital advertising beneficiary. The divergence between GOOG and META over such a short horizon underscores the market’s growing discrimination within the hyperscaler complex, where capital is rotating toward perceived under‑owned AI infrastructure winners and away from names seen as fully priced on near-term ad strength.

Outside of technology, the tape showed a clear bias toward cyclicals and operating leverage plays at the expense of defensives. Caterpillar (CAT) rose 7.1% this week and 21.8% over the month, Comfort Systems (FIX) added 8.2% and 30.7%, and Nucor (NUE) gained 5.5% and 30.1%, all signaling an appetite for infrastructure, construction, and industrial demand exposure. In contrast, The Clorox Company (CLX) fell 11.7% this week and 16.4% over the month, while Mondelez (MDLZ) was one of the few consumer staples names to post a positive week, up 6.5% and 7.5% over the month. Within medical devices and related health exposures, weakness in GE HealthCare (GEHC), down 11.3% on the week and 15.2% on the month, and Zimmer Biomet (ZBH), down 9.2% this week and 8.9% this month, reflects a continued derating of rate-sensitive, longer-duration cash-flow names.

Commodity-linked exposures sent mixed signals. In gold and precious metals, Newmont (NEM) dropped 10.0% this week and 4.5% over the month, while Agnico Eagle Mines (AEM) fell 8.3% and 12.6%, suggesting waning enthusiasm for gold-centric inflation hedges in favor of growth and cyclicality. In base metals, Freeport-McMoRan (FCX) declined 7.4% on the week and 7.6% over the month, while steel producer Nucor, as noted, rallied strongly. Energy was more balanced: Diamondback Energy (FANG) gained 6.6% on the week and 8.9% on the month, Devon Energy (DVN) advanced 5.5% and 4.0%, and California Resources (CRC) added 5.6% and 3.5%, indicating that upstream oil and gas remains a favored way to express a constructive macro view, even as some materials names lag.

The factor picture across the watchlist is consistent with a market leaning into growth, cyclicality, and AI beneficiaries while de-emphasizing defensive sectors, gold miners, and a subset of consumer staples. At the same time, dispersion remains high even within favored areas, as highlighted by the significant drawdown in POET Technologies (POET), down 51.6% on the week despite a 30.5% gain over the month, and sharp declines in Ch eck Point (CHKP), down 15.0% on the week and 21.4% on the month, and GLW, down 10.0% on the week and up 11.2% on the month. For portfolio construction, this implies that sector calls alone are insufficient; security selection, sensitivity to positioning, and catalyst mapping are increasingly critical.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

### Technology, AI, and Semiconductor Complex

The dominant narrative across the watchlist remains the interplay between AI infrastructure demand, legacy semiconductor cyclicality, and valuation dispersion within the broader technology complex. This week’s sharp gains in Intel, Seagate, Micron, and Western Digital highlight a renewed willingness to pay for cyclical leverage into data center, AI, and high-performance computing cycles. Intel’s 20.7% weekly move and 107.4% monthly appreciation suggest that investors are repricing the company’s foundry and CPU roadmap from skepticism to at least conditional optimism, especially as the market looks for incremental AI alternatives and diversification beyond the current GPU leaders. The magnitude of the monthly move implies a re-rating that likely assumes improving execution and better-than-feared margin trajectories, heightening the importance of forthcoming operational updates and any additional disclosures on AI acceleration strategy.

Seagate’s 24.0% weekly and 71.8% monthly gains, alongside Western Digital’s 6.8% weekly and 44.9% monthly performance, underscore a growing conviction that traditional storage is undergoing a demand renaissance driven by AI training and inference workloads, data proliferation, and continued cloud-scale capex. The market appears to be extrapolating a multi-year pricing and volume cycle for both HDD and NAND, even as investors differentiate between players on balance sheet quality and product mix. Micron, with a 9.2% weekly gain and 47.4% monthly move, remains a central beneficiary of high-bandwidth memory and next-generation DRAM, and the strength in its equity performance indicates that the market continues to treat it as a high-beta proxy for the AI infrastructure cycle.

At the same time, not all semiconductor and related names participated. Teradyne’s 17.4% weekly decline, despite being up 10.6% over the month, suggests rotational profit-taking in test equipment following strong gains and possibly concerns about order linearity or cyclicality as capex intentions are updated across chipmakers. ARM’s 10.1% weekly decline after a 36.2% monthly gain similarly reflects the market’s delicate balance between enthusiasm for its architecture and licensing leverage and a recognition that expectations had become elevated. The collapse in POET, with a 51.6% weekly decline despite a 30.5% monthly gain, exemplifies the fragility of sentiment in smaller, higher-risk semiconductor stories where liquidity and positioning can amplify both directions of the move.

Elsewhere in semis and specialty hardware, Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) advanced 8.7% for the week and 16.5% over the month, signaling ongoing appetite for specialty foundry capacity and differentiated process technologies. Lumentum (LITE), up 7.8% this week and 24.2% this month, is benefiting from renewed optimism in optical components tied to AI data center build-outs and hyperscale networking upgrades. Credo Technology (CRDO) offers another window into this theme: despite a 5.5% weekly decline, it remains up 92.2% over the month, reflecting the market’s eagerness to own high-speed connectivity names leveraged to AI infrastructure – though the weekly pullback highlights elevated volatility as investors rebalance exposures after outsized gains.

### Software Infrastructure, Cloud, and DevOps

Software infrastructure and cloud-related names also saw a decisive shift toward higher-beta, AI-adjacent platforms, with a strong bid in edge networking, observability, and developer tooling. Fastly (FSLY) rallied 18.1% on the week, though it remains down 13.3% on the month, signaling that the recent move is at least partially a recovery from prior drawdowns rather than a pure breakout to new highs. Cloudflare (NET) gained 5.0% on the week and 5.9% on the month, and DigitalOcean (DOCN) added 8.0% and 17.3% over those intervals, respectively, indicating that investors continue to favor platforms that can monetize AI workloads via bandwidth, security, and developer services.

Observability and data-monitoring names also outperformed. Datadog (DDOG) climbed 8.5% this week and 18.4% over the month, while Dynatrace (DT) gained 6.6% on the week and 2.3% on the month. These moves underscore the thesis that as AI-driven and cloud-native workloads proliferate, enterprises will need to invest in observability to maintain reliability and performance, giving these platforms durable, usage-based growth vectors. DevOps names showed similar strength: GitLab (GTLB) rose 11.8% this week and 9.4% over the month, and JFrog (FROG) advanced 10.2% and 3.0%, reinforcing the importance of software delivery automation and artifact management in modern development pipelines.

Cybersecurity performance was more balanced, highlighting a rotation within the group. Check Point (CHKP) declined 15.0% this week and 21.4% this month, a notable underperformance that likely reflects both competitive concerns and positioning unwinds. In contrast, Varonis (VRNS) gained 8.0% on the week and 21.9% on the month, Rapid7 (RPD) rose 6.7% and 16.7%, Tenable (TENB) increased 6.0% and 24.5%, and Rubrik (RBRK) added 5.3% and 13.3%. Qualys (QLYS) posted a 5.0% weekly gain. This dispersion suggests that the market is favoring growthier, cloud-native, and platform-centric security vendors over more mature or perceived slower-growth incumbents, with data-centric and identity-oriented security increasingly at the center of the investment narrative.

### Application Software and Collaboration

The application software cohort saw some of the most dramatic moves within the watchlist, as investors embraced names with clear levers to AI-enhanced productivity and evidence of improving operating discipline. Twilio’s 27.5% weekly surge and 40.5% month-to-date move indicate that the market is rewarding its efforts to streamline operations, pivot toward higher-margin products, and embed AI in communications workflows. Atlassian’s 24.2% weekly and 28.1% monthly gains point to renewed enthusiasm for its developer and collaboration ecosystem, with investors likely assigning more value to its ability to cross-sell, expand seat counts, and monetize AI features across Jira, Confluence, and related products.

Zoom’s 12.4% weekly and 28.2% monthly gains reflect a shift in sentiment from viewing it purely as a pandemic beneficiary to recognizing the potential of its broader collaboration and communications platform, particularly as AI features like intelligent summaries, transcription, and meeting analytics gain traction. BlackLine (BL), up 10.7% on the week but still down 7.0% on the month, appears to be in the early stages of a potential inflection, as investors re-evaluate its role in automating back-office financial workflows. HCM and payroll leader ADP rose 9.0% this week and 6.4% this month, a more measured but notable gain that aligns with ongoing interest in steady, recurring-revenue platforms with operating leverage.

Work management and productivity names delivered solid yet more moderate performance than the standout collaboration leaders. Asana (ASAN) advanced 9.4% on the week and 10.4% on the month, Monday.com gained 7.3% and 6.8%, and RingCentral (RNG) rose 10.2% and 18.2%. Collectively, these moves indicate that the market is willing to re-rate names where AI features can deepen engagement and drive upsell into higher tiers, provided that management teams demonstrate discipline on spending and a path to margin expansion.

### Consumer, Staples, and Defensive Rotation

Consumer staples and defensive consumer names saw meaningful dispersion, reflecting a broader rotation out of steady, bond‑like equities and into growth and cyclicals. The Clorox Company’s 11.7% weekly decline and 16.4% monthly drawdown mark one of the most pronounced underperformances within our consumer bucket, underscoring the degree to which the market is de-rating defensive staples amid shifting macro expectations. At the same time, Mondelez managed a 6.5% weekly gain and 7.5% over the month, and Unilever (UL) rose 2.8% this week, suggesting that not all staples are being treated equally; those with clearer pricing power, emerging-market exposure, or idiosyncratic catalysts may still attract capital.

Within home improvement and discretionary-related consumer exposures, Home Depot (HD) declined 3.6% over the week, while ecommerce and digital commerce platforms showed more resilience. Wix (WIX) gained 6.5% on the week despite being down 10.9% on the month, and Global-e (GLBE) was not listed among the major movers but sits within the broader digital commerce complex, where investors continue to seek exposure to cross-border ecommerce and merchant enablement. GigaCloud (GCT) fell 3.5% this week, highlighting the continued idiosyncratic nature of performance in more niche consumer-exposed growth names.

The rotation away from defensives was not limited to staples. In health-related defensives, GE HealthCare’s 11.3% weekly decline and 15.2% monthly drawdown, alongside Zimmer Biomet’s 9.2% weekly and 8.9% monthly declines, suggest that higher rates and concerns about hospital and capital equipment budgets continue to weigh on sentiment. In contrast, Elevance Health (ELV), a managed care and health services provider, rallied 8.1% on the week and 24.9% on the month, indicating that not all health exposures are being treated as bond proxies; insurers and services with visible cash flow and pricing power are being rewarded.

### Cyclicals, Materials, and Energy

Cyclical sectors delivered another week of outperformance within the watchlist, reinforcing the idea that investors are increasingly willing to own economically sensitive names alongside AI and growth. Caterpillar’s 7.1% weekly and 21.8% monthly rise is emblematic of this trend, as it provides leverage to global infrastructure, construction, and resource extraction. Comfort Systems (FIX) advanced 8.2% this week and 30.7% over the month, positioning it as a beneficiary of non-residential construction, HVAC, and energy-efficiency retrofits. In payments-linked industrial tech, Global Payments (GPN) rose 6.8% on the week and 10.7% over the month, benefiting from resilient consumer spending and digital payments penetration.

In materials, the week exposed a clear divide between steel and industrial materials versus precious metals and select specialty chemicals. Nucor’s 5.5% weekly gain and 30.1% monthly performance underscore the market’s constructive stance on steel demand and potentially more balanced supply conditions. Eastman Chemical (EMN) added 7.7% on the week and 2.3% on the month, reflecting some optimism around specialty chemical demand. By contrast, Newmont’s 10.0% weekly decline and 4.5% monthly drop, and Agnico Eagle’s 8.3% weekly and 12.6% monthly losses, indicate waning enthusiasm for gold miners as investors rotate into growth and cyclicals.

Energy names continued to grind higher, with Diamondback Energy up 6.6% on the week and 8.9% on the month, Devon Energy up 5.5% and 4.0%, and California Resources up 5.6% and 3.5%. These moves suggest that upstream producers remain favored as a way to express a constructive view on energy markets and cash-return frameworks. At the same time, GE Vernova (GEV), a power and utilities-oriented name, declined 7.5% this week despite being up 18.8% on the month, highlighting some near-term profit-taking in decarbonization and grid-related plays after their prior outperformance.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

### Extreme Moves: POET, Intel, Seagate, and Twilio

Among the most notable single-name moves on the watchlist this week, POET Technologies stands out with a 51.6% decline, even though it remains up 30.5% over the past month. Such a sharp round‑trip move over a short horizon is typical of smaller-cap names where expectations, liquidity, and positioning can shift rapidly. For fundamental investors, this type of volatility underscores the importance of sizing, liquidity awareness, and a clear thesis on the addressable market for POET’s photonics and chiplet technologies. The fact that the name is still positive over the month suggests that the market is wrestling with fundamentally positive developments or narrative shifts that have been partially overshadowed by positioning and profit-taking.

Intel’s 20.7% weekly gain and 107.4% monthly rally cement it as one of the most dramatic re-ratings in the large-cap semiconductor space. The magnitude of the move implies that investors are increasingly confident in the company’s foundry viability, manufacturing roadmap, and AI enablement, potentially viewing it as a necessary second source and complement to current GPU and accelerator leaders. For a buy-side portfolio, the key question is whether this re-rating has overshot near-term fundamentals or whether the market is only beginning to discount a multi‑year, multi-node improvement in its manufacturing competitiveness. In either case, the stock’s renewed momentum and sensitivity to news flow make it a focal point for both longs and hedges within the AI and semiconductor complex.

Seagate’s 24.0% weekly gain and 71.8% monthly performance similarly indicate a marked shift in expectations around storage demand and pricing power. The magnitude of the rally suggests that investors now see a higher baseline for AI-driven storage needs and a more benign supply environment than previously assumed. This re-rating can have second-order implications for peers like Western Digital, which, with a 6.8% gain this week and 44.9% over the month, is also being repriced as a beneficiary of the AI data wave. The asymmetry between Seagate’s and Western Digital’s weekly gains may reflect differing exposures to HDD and NAND, balance sheet considerations, or the market’s perception of execution risk.

In software, Twilio’s 27.5% weekly surge and 40.5% monthly move stand out. The market appears to be rewarding a combination of cost discipline, product focus, and expectations that messaging and communications APIs can benefit from AI features such as intelligent routing, personalization, and automation. For a stock with a checkered history of profitability and complexity in its product set, this type of re-rating suggests that investor skepticism is easing, at least for now. The key question going forward is whether Twilio can translate sentiment into sustained revenue acceleration and margin expansion, or whether this is primarily a positioning-driven squeeze after prolonged underperformance.

### Software Winners: Atlassian, Zoom, Monday, and Beyond

Atlassian’s 24.2% weekly gain and 28.1% monthly performance underscore investors’ renewed appreciation for durable, developer-centric platforms with multiple growth vectors. The stock’s move suggests that the market is increasingly comfortable with Atlassian’s ability to monetize AI features across its suite, drive deeper penetration into enterprises, and sustain high net revenue retention. Zoom, with a 12.4% weekly and 28.2% monthly gain, is being reinterpreted as a broader communications and productivity platform rather than a single-product video tool; its ability to embed AI copilots and intelligent features into its suite likely contributes to the re-rating.

Monday.com and Asana, up 7.3% and 9.4% this week (and 6.8% and 10.4% this month, respectively), provide a window into the market’s view of collaborative work management. Their gains suggest that investors see room for durable double-digit growth as enterprises standardize on a smaller set of workflow platforms and integrate AI to automate routine tasks. RingCentral’s 10.2% weekly and 18.2% monthly performance reflects a similar narrative in cloud communications, with AI potentially enhancing call analytics, routing, and customer engagement.

Amplitude (AMPL), a product analytics platform, posted a 10.3% weekly gain and 14.7% monthly performance, highlighting the role of data and experimentation in an AI-infused product landscape. As companies deploy AI features, understanding user behavior and iterating quickly becomes critical, which supports Amplitude’s long-term relevance. Across these names, the recurring theme is that AI is shifting from a buzzword to a concrete set of capabilities that can drive higher usage, better monetization, and, in some cases, expanded total addressable markets.

### Cybersecurity Divergence: Check Point versus Data and Cloud-Native Names

The cybersecurity cohort illustrates the growing divergence between incumbents and next-generation, cloud-native platforms. Check Point’s 15.0% weekly decline and 21.4% monthly drop stand in stark contrast to the gains seen in Varonis, Rapid7, Tenable, and Rubrik. Varonis, up 8.0% on the week and 21.9% on the month, benefits from heightened awareness of data security, insider threats, and compliance; Rapid7, with a 6.7% weekly and 16.7% monthly gain, is leveraged to detection and response; Tenable’s 6.0% weekly and 24.5% monthly performance reflects its exposure to vulnerability management and expanding cloud-security use cases; and Rubrik’s 5.3% weekly and 13.3% monthly move highlights the importance of data resilience and backup in a world of ransomware and data exfiltration.

The mixed performance underscores that security budgets remain healthy, but investor capital is rotating toward vendors perceived as structurally advantaged in cloud, data, and AI-assisted detection. The market appears to be increasingly unwilling to pay high multiples for slower-growing, appliance-centric models when cloud-native and data-centric alternatives can capture incremental spend. This dynamic may persist as AI continues to shape both the threat landscape and the tools used to defend against it.

### Defensive Laggards: Clorox, GE HealthCare, Newmont, and Others

On the downside, Clorox’s 11.7% weekly and 16.4% monthly declines, GE HealthCare’s 11.3% weekly and 15.2% monthly drawdowns, and Newmont’s 10.0% weekly and 4.5% monthly losses illustrate the pressure on defensive and yield-proxy names. For Clorox, the market may be de-rating its defensive premium amid more attractive opportunities in growth and cyclicals, especially if input costs stabilize and competitors regain shelf space. GE HealthCare, alongside Zimmer Biomet’s 9.2% weekly and 8.9% monthly declines, faces the dual headwind of rate sensitivity and concerns about capital equipment cycles and hospital spending priorities.

Newmont and Agnico Eagle’s 10.0% and 8.3% weekly declines, with a 4.5% and 12.6% monthly drop respectively, signal that gold miners are losing favor as investors find more compelling risk‑reward in AI, semiconductors, and cyclicals. While these names can still serve as hedges in a risk-off environment, the current rotation suggests that they may underperform in a scenario where growth, productivity, and disinflation narratives coexist and equity investors prioritize earnings growth over safe-haven attributes.

### Fintech and Financials: Steady but Selective

Fintech names on the watchlist posted respectable but less explosive moves compared with semis and high-beta software. Global Payments rose 6.8% this week and 10.7% this month, Affirm (AFRM) gained 6.0% and an impressive 48.3% over the month, and BILL Holdings advanced 5.1% on the week and 1.6% on the month. The strength in Affirm, in particular, points to ongoing enthusiasm for buy-now-pay-later penetration, as well as potential leverage to ecommerce and consumer resilience.

Traditional financials on the watchlist, such as Bank of America (BAC), Wells Fargo (WFC), and JPMorgan (JPM), delivered modest moves: BAC gained 2.3% on the week, WFC rose 1.8%, and JPM added 1.4%. American Capital Group (ACGL) declined 2.5% on the week, indicating some divergence within the financials complex. Overall, fintech and banks appear to be in a holding pattern compared with the more dramatic rotations in technology and cyclicals, but their stable performance can provide ballast within growth‑tilted portfolios.

## Macro & Rates Environment

The macro and rates environment over the past week, while not captured in precise numeric detail here, continues to serve as the backdrop for the observed factor rotations and sector dispersion. Equity investors appear to be embracing a scenario where growth remains resilient enough to support cyclical earnings, while inflation and policy concerns, though persistent, do not overwhelm risk appetite. This is reflected in the renewed appetite for semiconductors, industrials, and select financials, as well as the de-rating of rate-sensitive defensives such as long-duration medical devices and consumer staples.

From a positioning standpoint, the renewed strength in AI, semis, and high-beta software suggests that investors are again comfortable leaning into growth and duration, even as they trim exposures in perceived bond proxies. The outsized performance of names like Intel, Seagate, Twilio, and Atlassian indicates that the market is willing to look through near-term macro noise in favor of multi-year demand narratives tied to AI, digital transformation, and productivity gains. At the same time, the volatility in smaller-cap semis and speculative AI plays, such as POET and CRDO, underscores that liquidity and positioning can still drive short-term outcomes.

For portfolio construction, the key macro implication is that a barbell approach remains appropriate: maintaining exposure to secular AI and software winners while selectively owning cyclicals and quality financials, and funding these positions by trimming crowded defensives and gold miners. Without anchoring on specific yield levels, the observed rotation suggests that the market is at least temporarily comfortable with an environment where growth and disinflation can coexist, and where policy remains restrictive but not so much as to derail earnings. The risk, as always, is that an abrupt change in data or policy rhetoric could trigger a rapid unwind of growth and cyclicals, making risk management, hedging, and diversification crucial.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### 1. Intel (INTC)

Intel’s 20.7% weekly and 107.4% monthly performance represent one of the most significant re-ratings among large-cap technology names in our universe. The move suggests that the market has fundamentally shifted its expectations around Intel’s foundry prospects, competitive positioning in CPUs, and emerging role in AI acceleration. For years, Intel has traded at a discount to semiconductor peers due to execution missteps and manufacturing delays; the recent rally implies that investors now see a credible path to regaining process leadership or, at minimum, closing the gap sufficiently to compete effectively across data center, client, and AI workloads.

From a fundamental standpoint, the bull case rests on three pillars. First, the company’s foundry strategy, including external customer wins and potential government support, could transform Intel from a primarily integrated device manufacturer into a more diversified manufacturing platform. Second, its roadmap for CPUs and accelerators, including AI-enhanced products, may allow it to capture incremental share as customers seek alternatives to concentrated GPU supply. Third, operating leverage from higher utilization and improved execution could drive margin expansion, supporting the current re-rating. Given the magnitude of the move, we would be selective in adding at current levels, focusing on pullbacks or dislocations, while recognizing that the longer-term trajectory has clearly turned more constructive.

### 2. Seagate Technology (STX)

Seagate’s 24.0% weekly gain and 71.8% monthly surge underscore the market’s reassessment of storage as a structural AI beneficiary rather than a purely cyclical commodity. Historically, HDD demand has been tied to traditional enterprise and PC cycles, but the explosion of AI workloads, data retention requirements, and large language model training has dramatically increased the need for high-capacity storage. Investors now appear to be discounting a multi-year upcycle in capacity shipments and potentially more rational pricing, which can significantly enhance Seagate’s earnings power.

The key risks center on the sustainability of AI-driven demand and potential competition from alternative storage architectures. However, as long as hyperscale and enterprise customers continue to invest in data infrastructure, Seagate should maintain pricing power and utilization. The stock’s sharp move suggests that some of this optimism is now reflected in the price, but given the magnitude of the underlying secular shifts, we still see a constructive medium-term outlook, with pullbacks offering attractive entry points for long-term investors.

### 3. Micron Technology (MU)

Micron’s 9.2% weekly and 47.4% monthly gains reinforce its status as a core AI infrastructure beneficiary, given its exposure to DRAM, NAND, and particularly high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. The market is increasingly pricing in a robust demand environment, improving pricing, and a more disciplined supply landscape across memory peers. Micron’s leverage to AI training and inference workloads, combined with disciplined capex, positions it well to translate top-line growth into margin expansion.

For a buy-side portfolio, Micron remains a high-beta but compelling way to gain exposure to the AI infrastructure cycle. The key debate is where we are in the memory cycle; the strong month-to-date performance suggests that investors are looking beyond near-term inventory dynamics and focusing instead on a structural increase in bit demand. While volatility is likely to persist, especially around macro data and supply updates, the risk-reward remains attractive for investors with a multi-year horizon, particularly on pullbacks.

### 4. POET Technologies (POET)

POET’s 51.6% weekly decline, despite a 30.5% gain over the month, epitomizes the volatility inherent in smaller, higher-risk semiconductor and photonics names. The month’s net gain suggests that there have been positive developments or at least heightened expectations around its technology and commercialization roadmap, but the weekly drawdown points to either disappointment versus elevated expectations or profit-taking in a thinly traded name.

For institutional portfolios, POET’s profile necessitates careful sizing and a clear understanding of liquidity. The fundamental thesis likely revolves around its ability to enable more efficient photonic integration and chiplet architectures, which could be highly disruptive if successfully scaled. However, until there is greater evidence of volume adoption and predictable revenue, the name will remain highly sensitive to headlines, sentiment, and financing conditions. In practice, POET is better viewed as a satellite position within a broader AI and semiconductor basket rather than a core holding.

### 5. Twilio (TWLO)

Twilio’s 27.5% weekly and 40.5% monthly gains signal a significant shift in investor perception, after a prolonged period in which the stock struggled under the weight of profitability concerns and a complex product portfolio. The recent rally suggests that the market is increasingly confident in Twilio’s ability to rationalize its cost base, focus on higher-margin offerings, and embed AI across its communications and customer engagement stack. As enterprises seek to personalize interactions and automate workflows, Twilio’s APIs can serve as critical infrastructure, and AI can enhance its value proposition by improving targeting, routing, and analytics.

From a risk perspective, Twilio still needs to demonstrate that it can sustain durable growth while expanding margins, especially in a competitive landscape that includes both cloud hyperscalers and specialized CPaaS providers. However, the current re-rating could have legs if management continues to execute and if the broader software rerating persists. We would look to maintain or modestly increase exposure on weakness, recognizing that the stock’s beta and sensitivity to sentiment remain high.

### 6. Atlassian (TEAM)

Atlassian’s 24.2% weekly and 28.1% monthly performance reflects a robust re-rating of its collaboration and developer tools franchise. The company’s products, such as Jira and Confluence, are deeply embedded in software development and project management workflows, giving it strong competitive moats and high switching costs. Investors appear to be increasingly focused on Atlassian’s ability to layer AI capabilities on top of its existing products, improving productivity and making the platform even more central to its customers’ operations.

The company’s multi-product expansion and cloud migration also create opportunities for upsell and increased ARPU, which, combined with operating leverage, support the current valuation. That said, after the recent move, expectations will be higher, and any slowdown in cloud migrations or signs of macro-driven seat pressure could weigh on the stock. Nevertheless, Atlassian remains one of the higher-quality ways to express a belief in the durability of software development and collaboration as secular trends.

### 7. Zoom (ZM)

Zoom’s 12.4% weekly and 28.2% monthly gains suggest that the market is reassessing its post-pandemic narrative. Rather than viewing Zoom solely as a mature video conferencing tool, investors are giving more credit to its expanded platform, including Zoom Phone, Zoom Rooms, and AI‑driven features that can enhance productivity and meeting effectiveness. As hybrid work continues, Zoom’s opportunity lies in orchestrating communications across video, voice, and messaging, with AI acting as the connective tissue that turns interactions into actionable insights.

The re-rating brings Zoom back into focus as a potential compounder rather than a shrinking pandemic outlier. The key watchpoints will be enterprise adoption of its broader suite, competitive dynamics with other collaboration platforms, and its ability to maintain pricing power while investing in AI innovation. On balance, the recent move appears justified by an improving narrative, though we would continue to monitor execution closely before significantly increasing position sizes.

### 8. Alphabet (GOOG)

Alphabet’s 11.9% weekly and 29.9% monthly gains reflect a renewed conviction in its AI strategy, cloud momentum, and resilience of its core advertising business. The market appears to be re-rating Alphabet as a leading AI platform, both in terms of foundational models and applied AI across search, productivity, and cloud services. The stock’s move suggests that prior concerns about competitive threats in search and perceived delays in generative AI have eased, with investors now focusing on its ability to monetize AI features across its ecosystem.

Cloud remains a critical growth vector, and the recent performance implies growing confidence that Alphabet can sustain share gains and margin expansion in its cloud business. The company’s scale, data assets, and distribution give it multiple ways to benefit from AI adoption, and the stock’s recent appreciation aligns with that broad-based narrative. For portfolios, Alphabet remains a core holding in the AI and hyperscaler basket, with the main risk being whether the current pace of investment can be matched by monetization and margin progression over time.

### 9. Meta Platforms (META)

Meta’s 9.8% weekly decline, contrasted with a 5.1% monthly gain, highlights the near-term volatility in even the highest-quality megacap names. After a strong run, the stock appears to be experiencing profit-taking, possibly driven by concerns around the sustainability of ad pricing, regulatory scrutiny, or the capital intensity of its AI and metaverse investments. Nonetheless, the positive month-to-date performance indicates that the broader narrative around Meta as an AI and ad-tech leader remains intact.

For long-term investors, the key questions revolve around the balance between near-term margin pressure from AI and infrastructure investments and the longer-term monetization opportunities in AI-powered ads, commerce, and messaging. While the week’s pullback can be uncomfortable, it may also present selective opportunities to add, depending on risk tolerance and portfolio positioning, particularly for those underweight AI-enabled advertising.

### 10. Fastly (FSLY)

Fastly’s 18.1% weekly gain, despite a 13.3% monthly decline, positions it as a turnaround candidate within edge computing and content delivery. The recent move suggests that the market is starting to see signs of stabilization or improvement, possibly tied to new customer wins, product enhancements, or better cost control. Given its prior underperformance, even modest positive developments can catalyze sharp short-term rallies as short interest is covered and investors reassess the downside.

From a fundamental perspective, Fastly’s long-term value will depend on its ability to differentiate in performance, security, and developer experience versus larger competitors. AI workloads and real-time applications could play in its favor if it can position its edge network as a preferred platform for latency-sensitive use cases. However, the stock remains high risk, and we would treat the recent rally as an opportunity to reassess thesis progress rather than chase momentum blindly.

### 11. DigitalOcean (DOCN)

DigitalOcean’s 8.0% weekly and 17.3% monthly gains highlight its appeal as a developer-friendly cloud platform, particularly for small and mid-sized businesses. As AI tooling becomes more accessible, smaller developers and startups increasingly need affordable, simple infrastructure, and DigitalOcean is well positioned to serve that demand. The stock’s performance suggests that investors are recognizing its niche within the broader cloud ecosystem, distinct from the hyperscalers.

The key opportunity for DigitalOcean lies in bundling compute, storage, managed databases, and AI services in a way that remains intuitive and cost-effective for its target customer base. As long as it can sustain healthy net dollar retention and manage churn, the company can leverage operating scale to expand margins. The recent moves indicate growing confidence in that trajectory, though competitive pressures from larger clouds remain a longer-term risk.

### 12. Datadog (DDOG)

Datadog’s 8.5% weekly and 18.4% monthly gains reinforce its position as a core observability and monitoring platform leveraged to cloud, microservices, and AI-driven workloads. As systems become more complex, monitoring performance, reliability, and cost becomes critical, and Datadog’s breadth of products positions it as a strategic vendor. The stock’s performance suggests that investors continue to view it as a high-quality, durable grower even against a backdrop of macro uncertainty.

AI may further elevate Datadog’s relevance, as anomaly detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent alerting become more central to operations. The combination of usage-based pricing and an expanding product suite provides multiple paths to growth, though it also introduces some macro sensitivity if customers optimize spend. On balance, the current trajectory remains favorable, and Datadog remains a core holding within observability and infrastructure software.

### 13. Varonis (VRNS)

Varonis’s 8.0% weekly and 21.9% monthly gains highlight the increasing importance of data-centric security in a world of proliferating AI models and data repositories. As organizations store more sensitive data across cloud and on-prem environments, the risk of insider threats, misconfigurations, and external attacks rises. Varonis’s ability to classify, monitor, and protect data puts it at the center of this challenge.

The recent performance suggests that investors are recognizing its strategic positioning and are willing to re-rate the stock on expectations of sustained growth and margin improvement. AI may augment Varonis’s offerings by improving anomaly detection and automating policy recommendations. The main risk lies in execution and competitive dynamics, but the stock’s momentum reflects a constructive view on both fronts.

### 14. Rapid7 (RPD) and Tenable (TENB)

Rapid7’s 6.7% weekly and 16.7% monthly gains, alongside Tenable’s 6.0% weekly and 24.5% monthly performance, underscore the strength of vulnerability management and detection and response as core pillars of cybersecurity posture. Both companies benefit from regulatory and compliance drivers, as well as the secular need to manage risk in increasingly complex IT environments.

Their recent moves suggest that investors are willing to pay for growth and platform depth in security, especially as AI-enhanced threats increase the stakes. As these companies continue to expand their product footprints and integrate AI, they will likely remain important components of cybersecurity allocations. The ongoing underperformance of some legacy security vendors further reinforces the narrative that spend is consolidating around cloud-native platforms and data-centric solutions.

### 15. Nucor (NUE)

Nucor’s 5.5% weekly and 30.1% monthly gains make it a standout within the materials and steel space. The performance suggests that investors are increasingly constructive on steel demand, likely tied to infrastructure, construction, and reshoring-related investment. With a focus on efficiency and capital discipline, Nucor is well positioned to translate improved demand and pricing into strong cash generation.

The stock’s re-rating implies that the market sees this as more than a transient uptick, potentially reflecting a longer-term structural improvement in U.S. steel fundamentals. For portfolios that have been underweight materials in favor of technology and growth, Nucor offers an attractive way to add cyclical exposure without sacrificing balance sheet quality and capital-return discipline.

### 16. Caterpillar (CAT)

Caterpillar’s 7.1% weekly and 21.8% monthly gains underscore its role as a bellwether for global industrial activity. The move suggests that investors are increasingly confident in infrastructure spending, construction activity, and resource extraction, all of which drive demand for Caterpillar’s equipment. The company’s focus on high-margin services and parts adds resilience to its earnings profile, making it an attractive cyclical exposure.

The recent re-rating reflects expectations that mid-cycle earnings can move higher, especially if infrastructure programs and energy-related investment remain robust. For portfolios seeking cyclicality but cautious on balance sheet risk, Caterpillar remains a key candidate, though position sizing should account for its sensitivity to macro surprises and commodity cycles.

### 17. Diamondback Energy (FANG)

Diamondback’s 6.6% weekly and 8.9% monthly gains highlight the continued appeal of upstream energy names with disciplined capital allocation. The market appears to be rewarding producers that prioritize shareholder returns via dividends and buybacks while maintaining prudent investment in production. Diamondback’s exposure to prolific shale plays and its cost structure position it well to generate attractive free cash flow across a range of commodity price scenarios.

For growth-oriented portfolios, energy can serve as a diversifier and hedge against geopolitical and inflation risks. Diamondback’s performance suggests that investors view it as one of the higher-quality ways to gain that exposure. The key risk remains commodity price volatility, but the company’s framework for capital returns provides some downside mitigation.

## Upcoming Catalysts

Over the coming weeks, the absence of major earnings releases within the watchlist places greater emphasis on macro data, policy communications, and company-specific events such as investor days, product announcements, and AI roadmap updates. In technology and AI-related names, any incremental disclosures around capex plans from hyperscalers, cloud usage trends, and AI adoption metrics can act as catalysts, especially for semiconductors, data storage, and observability platforms. Companies like Intel, Micron, Seagate, and Western Digital are particularly sensitive to updates on data center and AI infrastructure spending intentions.

In software and cybersecurity, catalysts will likely revolve around product launches, AI feature rollouts, and commentary on demand trends from management teams at conferences and industry events. Twilio, Atlassian, Zoom, Datadog, GitLab, and Varonis, among others, may see sentiment shifts driven by evidence of AI monetization, customer wins, and improvements in net revenue retention. For security names like Check Point, Rapid7, and Tenable, any indications of budget shifts or consolidation trends among security platforms will be closely watched.

Within cyclicals, industrials, and materials, macro indicators of construction, manufacturing activity, and infrastructure spending will be key for names like Caterpillar, Nucor, and Comfort Systems. For energy, inventory data, OPEC+ commentary, and signals on demand will shape the near-term trajectory for Diamondback, Devon, and California Resources. In consumer and defensives, changing expectations around consumer spending, inflation, and rates will influence Clorox, Mondelez, Unilever, and similar names, especially as the market continues to rotate away from defensives toward growth and cyclicals.

## What To Watch Next Week

Looking ahead, the primary focus for buy-side investors should be on whether the current rotation into AI, semiconductors, and cyclicals can sustain without a meaningful setback in macro or policy expectations. The strength in Intel, Seagate, Micron, Twilio, Atlassian, and Alphabet points to a market that is willing to embrace risk and look through near-term volatility, but these moves also increase vulnerability to disappointments or abrupt shifts in sentiment.

We recommend closely monitoring flows and price action in key AI infrastructure names, including Intel, Micron, Seagate, Western Digital, and high-speed connectivity and optics plays such as Lumentum and Credo. Any sign of exhaustion or reversal in these names could signal a broader pause or consolidation in the AI trade. Similarly, continued strength in software and observability names such as Twilio, Atlassian, Zoom, Datadog, GitLab, and JFrog would reinforce the view that AI-driven productivity and developer tooling remain central to the investment narrative.

On the defensive side, we will watch whether the underperformance in Clorox, GE HealthCare, Newmont, and Zimmer Biomet stabilizes or accelerates. A stabilization could indicate that the rotation away from defensives has run its course for now, while further weakness might suggest more room for growth and cyclicals to run. In cyclicals and materials, the trajectory of Caterpillar, Nucor, Comfort Systems, and Diamondback Energy will provide a barometer for risk appetite toward economically sensitive sectors.

In summary, the week’s tape has reaffirmed AI, semiconductors, software, and select cyclicals as the primary engines of performance within our watchlist, while defensives and gold miners lagged. With no major watchlist earnings on the immediate horizon, the market’s focus will remain on macro developments, AI adoption signals, and company-specific catalysts. Portfolios should remain tilted toward high-quality AI and software leaders, balanced by selective exposure to industrial and energy cyclicals, and funded in part by trimming crowded defensives and gold miners, while maintaining sufficient diversification and hedging to navigate the elevated dispersion and volatility that continue to define this market regime.

market_summary:
US equities traded in a factor-driven tape, with semis, software, and select industrials sharply outperforming while defensives and some commodities lagged. Index-level performance was dominated by large-cap tech and AI leverage, even as individual names saw outsized dispersion, highlighted by dramatic swings in semiconductors and software infrastructure. Macro remained a secondary driver versus micro and positioning, with investors watching incoming inflation and Fed messaging for confirmation of a soft-landing path.
Rotation favored high-beta growth and cyclicals over staples and low-volatility exposures, as strong moves in names like INTC, STX, TWLO, and TEAM contrasted with drawdowns in POET, CHKP, CLX, and precious-metals miners. Beneath the surface, leadership broadened within software, data infrastructure, and industrials, while energy and materials were mixed. Looking ahead, the focus shifts to upcoming macro prints and Fed communication, which will help determine whether the current risk-on tone and AI-led rally can sustain into quarter-end.
